guided.title: Edit a shopping list
guided.prompt: The list `cart` holds `["milk", "eggs", "bread"]`. Add `"jam"` at the end, insert `"tea"` at index 1, then print the list and its length on two lines.
guided.starter:
cart = ["milk", "eggs", "bread"]
# change the list, then print it and its length
hints: `append()` adds to the end; `insert(index, item)` adds at a position.
After the `append`, call `cart.insert(1, "tea")`. Call the methods on their own lines.

guided.title: Remove and pop
guided.prompt: The list `queue` holds `["Ann", "Bo", "Cy", "Bo", "Di"]`. Remove the first `"Bo"`, then pop the last name and print it, then print the remaining list. Expected: the popped name on line 1 and the list on line 2.
guided.solution:
queue = ["Ann", "Bo", "Cy", "Bo", "Di"]
queue.remove("Bo")
last = queue.pop()
print(last)
print(queue)
hints: `pop()` with no argument removes and returns the last item, so store or print its result.

guided.title: Slice a list
guided.prompt: `nums` is `[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70]`. Print three lines, each a slice: the first three items, the last two items, and every second item starting at the first.
hints: A slice is `nums[start:stop:step]`; any part can be left out.
The last two items start at index `-2` and run to the end.

guided.title: Sort without changing the original
guided.prompt: `prices` is `[9.5, 3.0, 7.25, 3.0]`. Print the prices sorted from largest to smallest, then print the original list to show that it was not changed.
hints: One of the two ways to sort leaves the original list alone.
`sorted(list)` returns a new list, and `reverse=True` gives descending order.

independent.title: Trim the outliers
independent.prompt: The list `readings` is `[14, 9, 31, 22, 5, 18, 27, 12]`. Without changing `readings`, print on separate lines: a sorted copy; the sorted copy with its smallest and largest value removed (use a slice); and the average of that trimmed list rounded to 1 decimal place.
independent.solution:
readings = [14, 9, 31, 22, 5, 18, 27, 12]
ordered = sorted(readings)
trimmed = ordered[1:-1]
print(ordered)
print(trimmed)
print(round(sum(trimmed) / len(trimmed), 1))

independent.title: Working copy and rotation
independent.prompt: `days` is `["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri"]`. Make a separate copy called `rotated`. Move the first day of `rotated` to the end by removing it with `pop(0)` and appending it. Insert `"Sat"` at the end of the original `days`. Print `days`, then `rotated`, then `days[::-1]`, one per line.
independent.solution:
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri"]
rotated = days.copy()
rotated.append(rotated.pop(0))
days.append("Sat")
print(days)
print(rotated)
print(days[::-1])

independent.title: Top-three leaderboard (stretch)
independent.prompt: `scores` is `[64, 91, 78, 91, 55, 82]`. Print `Top 3:` and a space, then the three highest scores in descending order as a list. On the next line print `Best:` and a space, the highest score, and how many times it appears (separated by a space, using `max()` and `count()`). Then remove the first occurrence of the highest score and print the remaining list on a third line.
independent.solution:
scores = [64, 91, 78, 91, 55, 82]
print("Top 3:", sorted(scores, reverse=True)[:3])
best = max(scores)
print("Best:", best, scores.count(best))
scores.remove(best)
print(scores)

checks.question:
What does this print?

```python
items = [1, 2, 3]
result = items.append(4)
print(result)
```
checks.explanation: `append` changes the list in place and returns `None`, so `result` is `None`. The list `items` is the one that became `[1, 2, 3, 4]`.

checks.question:
What does this print?

```python
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)
```
checks.explanation: `b = a` gives the same list a second name; it is not a copy. Appending through `b` changes the one list that both names refer to.

checks.question: What does `[10, 20, 30, 40][1:3]` return?
checks.explanation: The start index 1 is included and the stop index 3 is not, so the items at indexes 1 and 2 are returned.

checks.question: Which statement gives a new sorted list and leaves `scores` unchanged?
checks.explanation: `sorted(scores)` returns a new list. `sort()` changes the list in place and returns `None`, so assigning its result loses the data.

checks.question:
What does this print?

```python
nums = [5, 6, 7, 8]
nums.pop(1)
print(nums[1])
```
checks.explanation: `pop(1)` removes the 6 and the later items shift left, so index 1 now holds 7. Index 1 does not still hold the removed item.
